live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming code planted on online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is the name for web card skimming: malicious JavaScript on checkout pages that copies payment details. Reports describe many groups, thousands of hit sites, and victims from Newegg to restaurants.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups use the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Malpedia's reference list carries headlines naming Magecart Groups 4, 8 and 12, as well as Keeper, ATMZOW, FIN6 and Mirrorthief.
WIRED says Magecart hackers cast the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Trend Micro cites Newegg, Ticketmaster and online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada as examples of sites hit.
A headline on Malpedia's list reports campaigns that infected 311 restaurants on online ordering platforms.
According to Malpedia, the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It relays card data to command and control servers.

Trend Micro lists three tactics: infecting third-party firms that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages. It says the record is 57 payment gateways.
One report says most Magecart attacks use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.

Malwarebytes found skimmers hosted on Heroku. A single injected line of code loads the script, a rogue iframe overlays the payment form, and stolen data is sent back encoded. Malwarebytes says the abusive instances were reported and taken down.
Sucuri describes the ATMZOW skimmer, which uses Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 it used heavy obfuscation and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.

RiskIQ reported that attackers registered a lookalike domain on August 13th, 2018, and the Newegg skimmer was active around August 14th. It was removed on September 18th, so shoppers were exposed for over a month.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer code is recognizable from the British Airways incident.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months. It names British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.

In October 2019, hackers breached Volusion, a provider of cloud-hosted online stores. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher. It calls this a Magecart-style supply-chain attack.
The same report says that in May 2019 hackers breached the cloud infrastructure of seven service providers to online stores. It traces those incidents to misconfigured cloud-hosting accounts.
Sucuri advises treating unexpected scripts as signs of compromise.
RiskIQ urged banks to review cards used on Newegg between August 14th and September 18th, 2018.
Store owners should keep a list of every script loaded on payment pages and check it often.
